threads.thread_goal: Align on current SME tax review workflow and main pain points.

messages.text: Kicking off the Standardised SME Tax Compliance Review Program channel. For T1 we need to map how we currently review SME tax files so we can consolidate into A1. Can each of you outline your usual steps from receiving the bookkeeping data through to final tax return, plus the main issues you hit most often?

My current flow for SME files is roughly: 1) Receive trial balance and bank statements from bookkeeping. 2) Check that ledgers tie to bank and VAT control. 3) Scan expenses for obvious non deductible items. 4) Post year end adjustments in a working spreadsheet. 5) Calculate tax and fill the return. 6) Save working papers in the client folder. Pain points: missing documents, unclear explanations for manual journal entries, and late adjustments from the manager after I thought the file was done.

My steps are similar but a bit more admin heavy: 1) Log receipt of the file in my own sheet. 2) Check that we have signed engagement and prior year return. 3) Compare current trial balance to prior year for big movements. 4) Review payroll and VAT returns for consistency. 5) Prepare tax calc in a spreadsheet and then copy into the tax software. Issues I see: I often do not know which source is the latest when there are multiple trial balances, and I spend time chasing basic info like director loan details.

I usually: 1) Confirm we have bookkeeping up to the year end and bank reconciliations. 2) Run a quick reasonableness check on revenue and margins versus prior year. 3) Review key balance sheet accounts: bank, debtors, creditors, VAT, payroll, loans. 4) Look at directors current accounts and dividends. 5) Review expense categories that are sensitive for tax, like travel, entertainment, and subcontractors. 6) Prepare the tax computation and attach supporting schedules. Main pain points: inconsistent documentation for loans and related party transactions, and unclear cut off around year end.

My flow: 1) Check client file for missing items using our intake checklist. 2) Confirm bookkeeping is closed and no one is still posting. 3) Export trial balance and detailed ledgers into a spreadsheet. 4) Do reconciliations for bank, VAT, and payroll. 5) Review P and L for unusual items and reclassify where needed. 6) Calculate tax and prepare the return. 7) Save a short summary of key judgements. Pain points: I often rework reconciliations because the format differs by clerk, and I do not always have a clear sign off point from the accounting manager.

Thanks all, this is helpful. I will start drafting A1 based on these flows. Before I do, can we agree on a single high level sequence, maybe 6 to 8 steps, that covers everyone? I am thinking: 1) Intake and completeness check. 2) Bookkeeping closure and reconciliations. 3) Analytical review versus prior year. 4) Detailed tax sensitive checks. 5) Tax calculation and return prep. 6) Internal review and sign off. 7) Filing and archiving. Does this reflect your reality, or are we missing a key step?
That sequence works for me. Maybe under bookkeeping closure and reconciliations we explicitly mention confirming no further postings after we start the review, since that is a recurring issue.
I like that structure. Could we also call out somewhere that we confirm engagement letters and prior year returns at intake? I sometimes only realise later that something is missing there.
Agree with the sequence. I would add that analytical review versus prior year should include both revenue and key expense ratios, not just balances, so we can spot margin anomalies early.

Works for me as well. For internal review and sign off, can we clarify that this includes manager review plus any adjustments, and only then we consider the file closed for filing? That would reduce the late change pain point.

Good points. I will update the draft for A1 to: 1) Intake and engagement check (including prior year). 2) Bookkeeping closure confirmation and reconciliations. 3) Analytical review versus prior year and key ratios. 4) Detailed tax sensitive checks. 5) Tax calculation and return prep. 6) Internal review, manager adjustments, and sign off. 7) Filing and archiving. Unless anyone objects today, I will treat this as our single current state workflow for T1.
No objections from me. That list matches how I work, just more clearly structured.
Fine by me as well.
Happy with that sequence.
Looks good to me too.

Next, we need to prioritise the main pain points so we can focus the new checklist and workflow on what matters most. From what you shared, I see: 1) Missing or late documents at intake. 2) Unclear or late manual journal entries and manager adjustments. 3) Inconsistent reconciliations and working paper formats. 4) Difficulty identifying the latest trial balance or source. 5) Weak documentation for loans, related parties, and directors accounts. Are these the top five we should target first for the new process?
Yes, that list captures my main headaches. If we can standardise reconciliations and make intake stricter, that would already save a lot of time.
Agree with those five. The only other one I would mention is unclear cut off around year end, but maybe that fits under reconciliations and documentation.
I am aligned. Cut off issues usually show up when we do reconciliations and analytical review, so I think we can handle that within those pain points.
Those five are the ones I see most often as well.

Great, then we will treat these as the top five pain points to address in the new checklist and workflow: 1) Intake completeness. 2) Manual journals and manager adjustments. 3) Standard reconciliations and working papers. 4) Single source of truth for trial balance. 5) Documentation for loans, related parties, and directors accounts. I will reflect this in A1 and use it as input for T2.

threads.thread_goal: Design and finalise the standard review checklist and spreadsheet template.

messages.text: I have drafted the first version of the SME tax review checklist for T2 and a matching spreadsheet template for T3. The checklist is in A2 and the spreadsheet in A3. Can you all take a look and share comments, especially on missing checks or confusing wording?

I went through A2. Overall it flows well. A couple of notes: 1) Under intake, could we add a tick box for confirming prior year tax return and computations are on file? 2) In the reconciliations section, maybe separate bank reconciliations from VAT and payroll so we can track them individually.

On A2, I am not sure I fully understand the risk flag about unusual director loan movements. Could we give an example or a threshold, like when the balance swings from debit to credit or exceeds a certain amount?

I checked A3. The structure with input, calculation, and summary tabs is good. One suggestion: in the input tab, can we lock the columns for account codes and descriptions and only allow entry in the amount columns? That would reduce accidental overwrites.

I tested A3 quickly with one anonymised file. The tax calculation formulas look correct, but I noticed that the rounding in the summary tab does not always match the tax software. We might want to round at the final tax figure only, not at each intermediate step.

Thanks for the feedback. I will add a specific line in the intake section for confirming prior year returns and computations, and I will split the reconciliations into separate items for bank, VAT, and payroll so we can see what is missing at a glance.

Good point on the director loan risk flag. I will rephrase it to something like: flag when the director loan balance changes sign compared to prior year or moves by more than a set threshold, and when there are frequent cash withdrawals without clear descriptions. We can refine the exact threshold later with the accounting manager.
On A3, I can protect the account code and description columns and leave the amount fields open. I will also add a short note at the top of the input tab explaining which cells are editable.
I will adjust the rounding so that we only round at the final tax figure in the summary tab. I will then retest with the same anonymised file to confirm it matches the tax software output.

One more thought on A2: should we have a separate section for documenting any tax positions that rely on judgement, like borderline expense classifications or relief claims, so that the manager review is focused there?

I like that idea. A short section for key judgements and assumptions would also help if an external auditor or tax inspector asks later. We could link it to the summary tab in A3 where we already show main adjustments.
Agreed. I will add a final section in A2 for key tax judgements and link it to a dedicated area in the summary tab of A3 where we can capture a short description and impact.
On the risk flags in A2, do we want to include anything specific for cash intensive businesses, like comparing declared cash sales to expected levels based on industry or card receipts?

That is a good call. Even a simple check like comparing cash takings to prior year and to card sales trends could highlight anomalies. We can phrase it as a risk flag without turning it into a full audit procedure.
I will add a risk flag in A2 for cash intensive businesses, focusing on unusual movements in cash sales compared to prior year and to card receipts, as suggested.
Once these edits are in, we should test A3 on at least three anonymised sample files as per T3. I have already used one; I can take two more and log any issues so we can fix them before the pilot.
Thanks, that would be helpful. Once you have tested on three files, we can treat the structure of A3 as fixed for the pilot, and only adjust formulas if we find errors.

I have now applied all the changes discussed to A2 and A3. Unless there are any strong objections by tomorrow morning, I suggest we treat the current version of A2 as the first usable checklist for the pilot under T2.
No objections from me. The checklist in A2 covers bookkeeping, tax calculation, documentation checks, and the main risk flags we identified.
I am happy to use the current A2 in the pilot.
Works for me as well.

Following the tests on three anonymised files, we have not found any structural issues with A3. I propose we lock the tab structure and key fields now for the pilot, and only correct formula errors if they appear.

threads.thread_goal: Define fraud indicators, escalation rules, and incident logging approach.

messages.text: I have put together an initial list of fraud indicators and draft escalation steps in A4 for T4. It covers things like unexplained cash movements, inconsistent VAT reporting, and unusual director loan activity. Can you review and suggest additional indicators or examples, especially where you have seen issues in practice?

In A4 I see indicators for cash and VAT, which is good. Maybe we should add something about repeated manual journals at month end that move expenses between accounts without clear descriptions, especially if they improve profit significantly.

Could we also include an indicator for customers or suppliers with duplicate bank details, or where the bank account is in a personal name rather than the business name? I have seen that raised by auditors before.
One more to consider: large or frequent round sum payments to the same counterparty without clear contracts or invoices. That often shows up in subcontractor or consultancy lines.

For escalation, A4 currently has three levels. I wonder if we should clarify when we just document in the file, when we raise internally to the accounting manager, and when we involve the compliance officer or external auditor. That would help us be consistent.
Good suggestion. I will add an indicator for repeated manual journals at period end that materially change profit or key ratios without adequate explanation or supporting documents.
I will also add an indicator for duplicate or unusual bank details on customer or supplier records, especially where the account is not in the entity name.
And I will include large or frequent round sum payments to the same party without clear contracts or invoices, as you mentioned.

On escalation thresholds, how about: Level 1: low impact or explainable items, just document in the file and note in the checklist. Level 2: items that could affect tax or financial statements but may have explanations, escalate to accounting manager for guidance. Level 3: strong indicators of intentional misstatement or potential fraud, escalate to compliance officer and, if they agree, to external auditor. We should also state that we do not contact clients directly about suspected fraud without manager approval.
That breakdown makes sense to me. It would help if A4 includes a short example for each level so we can classify cases more easily.
Agree, and I like the reminder not to contact clients directly about suspected fraud without approval. Maybe we should highlight that in bold in A4 so no one misses it.

I will update A4 to reflect the three escalation levels with examples, and I will add a clear note that any suspected fraud at Level 3 must be escalated to the accounting manager and compliance officer before any client contact.

We also need to agree on the incident log format for T11. I suggest we create a simple template with fields for client ID, date, description of indicator, level, actions taken, and outcome. That could live as a separate sheet linked from A4.
I can set up the incident log template for T11. I will include the fields you listed plus a reference to the relevant checklist item or working paper, so we can trace back easily.
For when to create an incident entry, should we say that any Level 2 or Level 3 case in A4 must be logged, while Level 1 items are just documented in the file?
That is a clear rule. I will add it to A4 and we can mirror it in the instructions for the incident log template.
Incident log template for T11 is now drafted with the agreed fields. I have also recorded a test incident using an anonymised example to check the flow.

I have now incorporated all the additional indicators and the three level escalation model into A4. Once the compliance officer reviews and confirms, I suggest we treat this as our final list of fraud indicators and escalation steps for the pilot.
With the incident log template in place and the rule that any Level 2 or 3 case in A4 must be logged, I think we can say we have agreed on the format and when to create an entry for T11.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and monitor the 30-file pilot execution and workload impact.

messages.text: I have created the draft pilot file register in A6 for T6, with space for 30 anonymised SME client IDs, industry, size, and review status. Please add candidate files you think are suitable for the pilot, keeping a mix of industries and complexity.

I have added six anonymised IDs for small retail and service clients that I know well. They are relatively straightforward and should be good for testing the checklist and A3 without too much extra complexity.
I have added five IDs for professional services and one small manufacturer. Let me know if the mix is ok or if we need to swap any out.
I added eight IDs, including some construction and hospitality clients where cash and subcontractor issues are more common. That should help us test the fraud indicators in A4 as well.

I have added the remaining IDs, focusing on a mix of small and medium sized clients across different sectors. We now have 30 entries in A6. I also checked that source documents are available for all of them.

Thanks all. The mix in A6 looks balanced across industries and sizes, and we have confirmed document availability. Unless anyone spots an issue, I suggest we freeze this list as our 30 pilot files for T6.
Freezing the list works for me.
Ok for me as well.
Agreed.
No issues from my side.

Next we need a realistic schedule for T7. We have 21 days total. If we each take around 7 to 8 files, that is roughly 2 to 3 files per week per person. Does that fit with your other deadlines if we timebox each review to, say, 2 hours using A2 and A3?
That sounds manageable for me. I can aim for three files per week, starting with the simpler ones I added to A6.

I have a couple of busy days with other filings, so I might only manage two files in the first week, then catch up with three per week after that. If needed, I can swap one of my more complex files with a simpler one.
I can take eight files, including some of the more complex ones, and aim for three in the first week and three in the second, leaving two for the final week as buffer.
I can handle seven files, targeting three in week one, two in week two, and two in the final week, leaving some time for template and checklist tweaks if we find issues.
I will take the remaining nine files and aim for three per week. I will also post a short weekly status summary in this channel so we can see progress against the 30 file target in A6.

Based on this, our schedule is: Week 1: around 11 to 12 files, Week 2: another 11 to 12, Week 3: remaining files and any rework. This should allow us to complete T7 within the 21 day deadline, assuming we stick to the timebox and use A2 and A3 consistently.
Schedule works for me. I will also make sure anonymisation rules in A5 are applied when we share any examples from the pilot.
All good from my side. I will start with two files today and update A6 as I complete them.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and agree on adjustments and rollout approach.

messages.text: I have drafted the pilot findings and process improvement report in A7 for T8, based on the 30 files logged in A6. It includes key error patterns, time taken per file, and suggestions for adjusting the workflow and checklist. Please review and add comments, especially if anything does not match your experience during the pilot.

In A7, the point about intake completeness matches what I saw. Files where the intake section of A2 was fully completed went much smoother. Maybe we should make some of those intake items mandatory before starting the review.

I agree with the finding in A7 that reconciliations took longer than expected on some files. I sometimes had to rework the bank reconciliation because the format was not clear. Maybe we can add a short example layout in A3 or a separate guidance note.

One thing I noticed that is not fully captured in A7 is that the fraud indicators in A4 were triggered a few times, but we were not always sure whether to log an incident or just document in the file. The Level 2 versus Level 3 distinction could use one or two more concrete examples.

On timing, A7 shows an average of about 1.8 hours per file once we got used to A2 and A3, which seems acceptable. For more complex files, it went up to 3 hours, but that was usually where documentation was weak. I think the process is workable within the monthly cycle if we plan ahead.

Good point. One of the improvement suggestions in A7 is to make certain intake items in A2 mandatory before starting detailed review, such as prior year returns, engagement letter, and confirmation that bookkeeping is closed. We can highlight those as must have items.

For reconciliations, we could add a simple example bank reconciliation layout in A3 or as an appendix to A7. That would help standardise how we present them without changing the main template structure.

I can draft two extra examples in A4: one where unusual cash movements are explainable and logged as Level 2, and one where there is strong evidence of intentional misstatement, which would be Level 3 and require an incident log entry.
Another observation: the key judgements section in A2 was very useful when the manager reviewed the file. Maybe we should make it more prominent in the training brief so new clerks do not skip it.

On integration with the monthly cycle, I found it easier when I blocked specific slots for pilot reviews rather than trying to squeeze them between other tasks. Maybe T12 can formalise that by suggesting when in the month we do these reviews.
I will make sure the training brief for T9 highlights the key judgements section in A2 and shows one or two examples from the pilot where it helped during manager review.

For T12, I propose we integrate the new review process as follows: for monthly clients, we perform the checklist and A3 review in the week after month end close; for annual only clients, we schedule the review at least four weeks before the filing deadline. I will align this with the accounting manager for confirmation.

On quality control, A7 suggests sampling a small percentage of files each month for a second review. Maybe T10 can define a simple rule, like 10 percent of SME files per month, with at least one file per clerk.
I can draft the QC sampling approach for T10. A rule like 10 percent of SME files per month, minimum one per clerk, sounds reasonable. I will align the QC checklist with A2 and put it into A8.

Given the feedback, I propose we approve the following key process changes from A7: 1) Make certain intake items in A2 mandatory before review. 2) Add a standard bank reconciliation example linked to A3. 3) Clarify Level 2 and Level 3 examples in A4 and ensure Level 2 and 3 cases are logged. 4) Integrate the process into the monthly cycle as outlined in T12. If everyone agrees, we can treat these as the approved changes coming out of the pilot.
I am happy with those changes. They reflect what I experienced during the pilot.
Agreed from my side as well.
I support these adjustments.

QC sampling rule for T10 is now drafted in A8 as 10 percent of SME files per month, minimum one per clerk, with a short QC checklist aligned to A2. I think this is feasible within our current workload.

The training brief for T9 is also drafted. It covers the workflow, A2, A3, A4, anonymisation rules in A5, and includes three examples from the pilot, including one where a fraud indicator led to an incident log entry.
With A8 and the training brief in place, I suggest we confirm that the QC sampling approach and training content are approved for rollout, subject to the accounting manager sign off on T9.
